c.v: Name four things that limit how fast a headless simulation runs. Then say which of the four a larger step size helps and which it does not, and name the command that tells you the rate a run actually achieved. Take 10 minutes.
Four, and they are the four you profile:

items.v: The physics of each step: how many bodies and joints there are, how many contacts the solver has to resolve, and how many iterations it takes to do it.

The sensors, and above all the ones that render. A camera or a GPU lidar has to draw the scene, which is the most expensive thing in most worlds and the reason a rendering world is the usual reason a run is slow.
The systems and their publishing: every plugin's three phases run on every step, and everything they publish is serialised and sent.
The machine: cores, memory bandwidth, and whether there is a GPU that the rendering can use at all.

c.v: A larger step helps the first, the third and the per-step part of the fourth, because there are fewer steps per simulated second and each of those costs is paid once per step. It does not help the sensors, because a sensor runs at its own rate in simulated time, so a 30 Hz camera renders thirty times per simulated second whether the step is 1 ms or 4. That asymmetry is the one to remember: doubling the step halves the physics bill and leaves the rendering bill exactly where it was.
The rate a run achieved comes from

You pass with four limits, the right split for the step size, and one of the two commands. Missing the sensor asymmetry is a partial pass, and it is the expensive one: it is the reason people spend a day tuning the step size on a world whose cost is a camera.

A simulation's speed is measured by its real-time factor: simulated seconds divided by wall seconds. A factor of one means it keeps up with the clock, and less than one means a ten-second scenario takes longer than ten seconds to run.

The problem is that the factor decides what you can afford to test. A continuous-integration job that runs twenty scenarios at a factor of 0.3 takes three times as long as the robot would, so either the job is slow enough that people stop waiting for it or the number of scenarios stops growing. It also changes the test itself, because the nodes outside the simulator run on wall time: a controller that needs five milliseconds of processor answers five milliseconds late at a factor of one and fifty milliseconds late at a factor of ten.

The mechanism is a budget per step. The simulator advances a fixed step of simulated time and paces itself so that one step takes one step's worth of wall time at the target factor. At a one-millisecond step and a target of one, everything that happens in a step has one millisecond of wall time to happen in: the physics solve, every loaded plugin's three phases, any sensor that is due, and the publishing. Miss the budget and the factor drops, and the lost time is not made up later.

The cost of getting it wrong is subtle. The two big levers pull against other things you want. A larger step buys speed and loses integration accuracy, which matters for anything stiff. Lower sensor rates buy more, because rendering usually dominates, and change what the robot's code receives.

Where you meet it is the first time a scenario times out in CI. The instinct is to raise the timeout. The right move is to measure where the step time goes, because the fix is usually a sensor you did not need for the claim the scenario is making, and removing it costs nothing.

c.v: The three numbers at the top are a profile, and they are the thing you have to measure on your own machine: this one has no Gazebo and no GPU, so the arithmetic is real and the inputs are an illustration. The shape of the answer is what transfers.

Read the lower table as a list of things people try. Removing the transport entirely, which is the change somebody always proposes because publishing looks wasteful, moves the factor from 0.83 to 0.96 and does not reach 1. Making the physics twice as fast, which is weeks of work if it is possible at all, reaches 1.01. Halving the sensor rates, which is one line in a model file, reaches 1.12 and beats both. And the step size, which costs nothing to change and costs accuracy to live with, gets to 1.31 on its own and to 2.20 combined with the sensor rates. The general rule is the old one about optimising: the component with the largest share bounds what any amount of work on the others can buy, and here the sensors are half the bill.
The four costs deserve a sentence each about where they actually come from.

scales with the number of bodies and joints, and worse with the number of contacts, because contacts are what the constraint solver spends its iterations on. A robot standing still on a flat floor has a handful; the same robot in a room full of scattered objects has many, and the cost is not linear in the object count but in how many of them are touching. This is also the cost that a larger step reduces most directly, and the one whose accuracy a larger step damages, which the time-stepping topic measured for a stiff system.

Two things drive it, the image size and the rate, and both are numbers in the model file. A GPU lidar with 360 samples is cheap; a 640 by 480 camera at 30 Hz is not; a depth camera is the same work again.

It becomes the bottleneck only when somebody bridges a camera topic to ROS, at which point the bridge is copying megabytes a second between two processes and the cost has moved out of Gazebo where none of your Gazebo measurements will find it.

Meshes and textures are what fill it, so a world assembled from detailed models can need gigabytes that the same world in primitives does not.

One number ties this to the bench.

scenario's plan is 2 s of warm-up, 3 s of driving and 3 s of settling, so 8 s of simulated time. At a factor of 0.83 that is under 10 s of wall time and the 180 s cap is irrelevant. The run alone reaches the cap at a factor of 8 divided by 180, which is 0.044. The cap covers more than the run, though: Gazebo has to start, the world has to load and the nodes have to discover each other before the first sample arrives, and none of that scales with the factor. Measure that start-up on your own machine, because it is the term this arithmetic turns on; if it takes 45 s, the run has 135 s left and the factor has to stay above 8 divided by 135, which is 0.059. So the real-time factor is more than a convenience: somewhere around 0.06 on a machine with that start-up, this scenario stops testing the robot and starts testing the timeout, and a run that fails that way needs a different diagnosis from one that fails a check.

is the prediction you check your model against: it should come out near half the per-step part plus the whole of the sensor part, and if it does not, something else changed with the step size and the profile is not yet the right shape.

Which lever to pull follows from the shares, not from preference. If the sensors are more than half the bill, as they are in the illustration above, then no amount of work on the physics gets you to a factor of 1, and the two changes worth making are the sensor rate and the step size. If the sensors are a small share, the step size is the only lever with any reach and its cost is accuracy. Either way, name the claim the scenario makes before cutting a sensor: a lidar the scenario's checks never read is free to remove, and one the robot steers by is not, which is the fidelity topic's question arriving inside a performance decision.

Step 4. A real update rate below the nominal means the sensor is not being served at the rate it asked for, which happens when the render of the previous update has not finished when the next is due. It does not mean the simulated rate is wrong: the simulated update rate can be exactly nominal while the real one is a third of it, and that combination is the normal state of a healthy run at a factor of one third. The number that tells you about the simulation's correctness is the simulated rate; the number that tells you about its speed is the real one. Reading the second as the first is the mistake this measurement exists to prevent.
Step 5, the first question. Run the same world twice, once as it is and once with

on a machine with no display, and compare; then run with every rendering sensor removed and compare again. If removing the sensors changes the wall time a lot and the two rendering modes differ a lot, the graphics path is the limit. If neither changes much while the processor sits at 100% of one core, the limit is the physics on a single thread, which no graphics card will help with.

The second question. Without a GPU the rendering runs in software, so the sensors' share of the bill is larger than the illustration and the ordering of the levers is more strongly in their favour: cutting a sensor rate buys more, and improving the physics buys even less than the table shows. It also means a number measured on your machine does not transfer to a machine with a GPU, and the honest way to report a performance result is with the hardware named next to it, which is the same rule the reproducibility topic gave for every other number a run produces.
